lesson.title: Degrees ↔ radians
lesson.body:
π rad = 180°, so 1 rad ≈ 57.3° and 1° ≈ 0.01745 rad.

  • Nice angles: reduce the fraction of 180°. 135° = 135/180 · π = 3π/4 ≈ 3 × 0.785 = 2.356. Know π/12 ≈ 0.262, π/6 ≈ 0.524, π/4 ≈ 0.785, π/3 ≈ 1.047, π/2 ≈ 1.571.
    Back the other way, π/n = 180°/n: 5π/6 = 5 × 30° = 150°.
  • Any angle → rad: start from the nearest nice angle and add 0.01745 per extra degree. 37° = 30° + 7° ≈ 0.524 + 0.122 = 0.646. Or ÷ 57.3, or × 0.0175 (= 7/400) and shave 0.3%.
  • rad → °: × 57.3, split into whole and fractional parts: 2.3 rad = 2 × 57.3 + 0.3 × 57.3 = 114.6 + 17.2 ≈ 131.8°.

Sanity anchors: 1 rad is a bit under 60°; 3 rad is just under 180°; 6.28 rad is a full turn.

lesson.title: Trig values
lesson.body:
1. Unit circle symmetry. Any angle reduces to a reference angle in 0–90°; only the sign changes. Signs by quadrant: ASTC — All positive in I, Sin in II, Tan in III, Cos in IV. Negative angles: add 360° (cos is even, sin and tan are odd).
225° = 180° + 45° (III) → sin 225° = −√2/2 ≈ −0.707; cos(−30°) = cos 30° ≈ 0.866.

2. In-between angles: anchor + slope. Go from the nearest memorized angle (0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90°) using the derivative, with the step in radians (1° = 0.01745):

  • sin(a + d) ≈ sin a + cos a · d
  • cos(a + d) ≈ cos a − sin a · d
  • tan(a + d) ≈ tan a + (1 + tan² a) · d

sin 37°: 7° ≈ 0.122 rad → 0.5 + 0.866 × 0.122 ≈ 0.606 (true 0.602; the curve bends down, so a linear step slightly overshoots).

3. Radian arguments. Small x: Taylor — sin x ≈ x − x³/6, cos x ≈ 1 − x²/2, tan x ≈ x + x³/3 (sin 0.4 ≈ 0.4 − 0.011 = 0.389). Larger x: use radian anchors π/6 ≈ 0.524, π/4 ≈ 0.785, π/3 ≈ 1.047, 5π/12 ≈ 1.309 with the same slope rule — no degree conversion needed: cos 1.2 ≈ 0.5 − 0.866 × 0.153 ≈ 0.368. Past π/2, fold: sin x = sin(π − x), cos x = −cos(π − x).

lesson.title: Small-angle approximations
lesson.body:
For a small angle θ in radians:

  • sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ (relative errors θ²/6 and θ²/3)
  • cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2, i.e. 1 − cos θ ≈ θ²/2

Even at 10° (θ ≈ 0.175) sin θ ≈ θ is off by only 0.5% and tan θ ≈ θ by 1%; refine with θ(1 − θ²/6) or θ(1 + θ²/3). Degrees first: θ = x° × 0.01745 (or x ÷ 57.3).

Example: sin 2.5° ≈ 2.5 × 0.01745 ≈ 0.0436. 1 − cos 4°: θ ≈ 0.0698, θ² ≈ 0.00487 → 0.00244.

Arc length: an object of size s at distance d (s ≪ d) subtends θ ≈ s/d radians = 57.3 · s/d degrees. Equivalently, something 1 unit wide at 57.3 units away spans 1°.

  • 1.8 m person at 2.5 km: 1.8/2 500 = 0.00072 rad × 57.3 ≈ 0.041°
  • The Moon: 3 474 km / 384 400 km ≈ 0.0090 rad ≈ 0.52°; a thumb at arm's length ≈ 2°.
  • Reverse: size ≈ θrad · d; distance ≈ 57.3 · s / θ°. Watch the units (m vs km)!

lesson.title: Inverse trig
lesson.body:
Exact values are your special-angle table read backwards; give the answer in the principal range: arcsin and arctan in −90°…90° (both odd: arcsin(−x) = −arcsin x), arccos in 0°…180° with arccos(−x) = 180° − arccos x.
arccos(−0.866) = 180° − 30° = 150°; arctan √3 = 60°; arcsin(−1/2) = −30°.

Extra anchors worth memorizing (3-4-5 triangle and friends):

  • arcsin 0.6 = arctan 0.75 = 36.87°; arcsin 0.8 = arctan 4/3 = 53.13°
  • arctan 0.5 = 26.57°; arctan 2 = 63.43°

In between: anchor + inverse slope. d(arcsin x)/dx = 1/cos θ and d(arctan x)/dx = 1/(1 + x²), in radians — multiply by 57.3 for degrees.
arctan 0.3: anchor tan 15° = 0.268, slope 1/(1 + 0.268²) ≈ 0.933 rad ≈ 53.5°/unit → 15° + 0.032 × 53.5° ≈ 16.7°.
arcsin 0.55: 30° + 0.05 × (57.3/0.866) ≈ 30° + 3.3° = 33.3°.

Small x: arcsin x ≈ arctan x ≈ x rad = 57.3·x degrees (arctan 0.15 ≈ 8.6°). arccos x = 90° − arcsin x: arccos 0.2 ≈ 90° − 11.5° = 78.5°.
